title: Isaiah 5:1–7
context: Isaiah sings for his beloved a song of a vineyard on a fertile hill. The beloved digs, clears stones, plants choice vines, builds a tower, hews a vat, and looks for grapes. Wild grapes come. Jerusalem and Judah are told to judge. What could have been done more to do? The hedge will be removed, the wall broken, briers will grow, the clouds commanded not to rain. The vineyard is the house of Israel; Judah his pleasant planting. He looked for justice, and behold, bloodshed; for righteousness, an outcry.

voices.heading: Voices from both camps
voices.intro: On a well-dressed vineyard that yielded wild grapes, a few classic voices from each tradition.
voices.note: Quotations lightly abridged for length; wording follows standard English translations of the sources named.

arminian.quote: Now—I will record it to be a witness for God, and against you, as Moses did his song. Vineyard—his church. He gathered—he removed all hindrances, and gave them all the means of fruitfulness. A tower—for the residence of the keepers. Nor digged—I will remove my ministers, who used great care and diligence to make you fruitful. Thorns—I will give you up to your own lusts. No rain—I will deprive you of all my blessings. Pleasant—in whom God formerly delighted. A cry—from the oppressed, crying to men for help, and to God for vengeance.
arminian.source: Explanatory Notes upon the Old Testament (on Isa 5:1–7)

reformed.quote: What more ought to have been done to my vineyard? He inquires what could have been expected from the best husbandman which he has not done. Hence they had no excuse. If it be objected that God had the remedy in his hands, if he had turned the hearts of the people, this is an idle evasion as applied to those men; for their conscience holds them fast. Though God do not pierce the hearts of men by the power of his Spirit, so as to render them obedient to him, yet they will have no right to complain that this was wanting; for every pretense of ignorance is taken away by the outward call. Besides, God does not speak here of his power, but declares that he was not under any obligation to do more than he did. God, to whose eyes all things are naked, is not deceived by his expectation like a mortal man.

verses.text: Let me sing for my well beloved a song of my beloved about his vineyard. My beloved had a vineyard on a very fruitful hill.
verses.arminianNotes:
Let me sing for my well beloved a love song concerning his vineyard: a vineyard on a very fruitful hill. Wesley: a witness for God and against you, as Moses’ song; vineyard—his church; hill—places most commodious for vines.

Judah as the beloved’s plot. A hill, a love. The singer is jealous for the bride entrusted to him.
verses.reformedNotes:
Calvin: a poem in behalf of God, that he might expostulate about ingratitude. Beloved: God; Isaiah assumes the character of one jealous for the bride. Vineyard: no dearer possession, and none that demands more constant toil. Hill, son of oil: a fertile situation in the allegory, the people’s prosperous condition under care.

The care is His peculiar regard, not common rain on just and unjust. Either reading: beloved, vineyard, fertile hill.

verses.text: He dug it up, gathered out its stones, planted it with the choicest vine, built a tower in the middle of it, and also cut out a wine press in it. He looked for it to yield grapes, but it yielded wild grapes.
verses.arminianNotes:
He dug it, cleared stones, planted choice vines, built a watchtower, hewed a wine vat; he looked for grapes, and it yielded wild grapes. Wesley: he removed all hindrances and gave them all the means of fruitfulness; a tower for the keepers.

Means actually given. Choice vines were planted; wild grapes still came. The looking is not a fake warning. All the ordinary care of a husbandman was there; the yield was theirs.
verses.reformedNotes:
Calvin: incessant care; he has neglected nothing expected of the best householder. Do not force every clause (Spirit as fence, doctrine as vat). Planted, then everything else necessary. He hoped it would bring forth grapes: God is not deceived like a mortal (Heb 4:13); Isaiah describes how the people ought to have acted. The gospel is proclaimed for the obedience of faith, not because He expects all to be obedient, but that unbelievers are rendered inexcusable by the hearing.

The looking names their duty, not a gap in His knowledge. Stones, choice vines, tower, vat, wild grapes.

verses.text: “Now, inhabitants of Jerusalem and men of Judah, please judge between me and my vineyard.
verses.arminianNotes:
Now, inhabitants of Jerusalem and men of Judah, please judge between me and my vineyard. Hearers are made the jury.

“Judge”—an appeal to historical men of Judah. They can still weigh the case. The vineyard is theirs to recognize.
verses.reformedNotes:
Calvin: the guilty are made judges in a cause so plain they have no evasion. Proof of the strongest confidence: bid them declare if this be not the fact. Immediately the accusation is decided against those to whom he now commits the decision.

Their own mouth will close the plea. Jerusalem, Judah, judge between me and my vineyard.

verses.text: What could have been done more to my vineyard, that I have not done in it? Why, when I looked for it to yield grapes, did it yield wild grapes?
verses.arminianNotes:
What could have been done more to my vineyard, that I have not done in it? Why, when I looked for grapes, why wild grapes? Wesley’s “all the means of fruitfulness” stands here: nothing ordinary was withheld.

“What more could have been done?” Arminian readers find in God’s question a sincere lament: every means of fruitfulness was given, and the wild grapes were still the vineyard’s own yield.
verses.reformedNotes:
Calvin: what could have been expected from the best husbandman which he has not done? They have no excuse. If it be objected that God had the remedy in his hands, if he had turned their hearts, this is an idle evasion; conscience holds them. Though God do not pierce hearts by His Spirit so as to render them obedient, they cannot complain that this was wanting; the outward call takes away ignorance. He does not speak here of His power, but declares He was not obligated to do more than He did.

The complaint stops their mouth; it does not teach that effectual turning was omitted as if He lacked it. Both sides agree: what more, looked, wild grapes.
verses.keyContrast: Both confess the Lord did all a vineyard’s husbandman does, and that Judah’s wild grapes are without excuse (5:4). Arminians hear all the means of fruitfulness actually given, and a looking that wild grapes disappointed (Wesley). Calvinists hear no proof that God failed to turn the heart: He does not speak here of His power to pierce; the outward call leaves them inexcusable, and He was not obligated to do more (Calvin).

verses.text: Now I will tell you what I will do to my vineyard. I will take away its hedge, and it will be eaten up. I will break down its wall, and it will be trampled down.
verses.arminianNotes:
I will take away its hedge, and it will be eaten up. I will break down its wall, and it will be trampled down. After the verdict, the sentence.

“Hedge”—walls of Judah coming down—Assyria, then Babylon—not a slogan against borders. Protection withdrawn is still His doing; trampling is still armies’.
verses.reformedNotes:
Calvin: vengeance for contempt of grace. They will be deprived of the gifts they abused. When His protection is gone they become prey to all that pass by, men or beasts.

He withdraws what He put up. Both traditions see: hedge, devour, wall, trample.

verses.text: I will lay it a wasteland. It won’t be pruned or hoed, but it will grow briers and thorns. I will also command the clouds that they rain no rain on it.”
verses.arminianNotes:
I will lay it a wasteland; not pruned or hoed; briers and thorns; I will command the clouds that they rain no rain on it. Wesley: I will remove my ministers who used care to make you fruitful; thorns—give you up to your own lusts; no rain—deprive you of all my blessings.

Drought and neglect of the plot. Ministers withdrawn, lusts unpruned. The clouds still hear Him.
verses.reformedNotes:
Calvin: He will not take pains to dig and prune; briars choke; by withholding rain He dries the roots. Weapons for punishing ingratitude. Whenever we are justly deprived of favors freely bestowed, acknowledge His anger.

The same hand that commanded rain now commands none.

verses.text: For the vineyard of the LORD of Armies is the house of Israel, and the men of Judah his pleasant plant. He looked for justice, but behold, oppression, for righteousness, but behold, a cry of distress.
verses.arminianNotes:
The vineyard of the LORD of Armies is the house of Israel, and the men of Judah his pleasant planting; He looked for justice, behold, bloodshed; for righteousness, behold, an outcry. Wesley: pleasant—in whom God formerly delighted; a cry from the oppressed, to men for help and to God for vengeance.

The riddle of the vineyard is now explained. Justice was looked for in the gates (1:23; 3:14). Bloodshed and cry are theirs. The looking of v. 2 is now justice and righteousness.
verses.reformedNotes:
Calvin: without metaphor now. Whole nation the vineyard, individuals the plants; no man escapes. He looked for judgment, behold oppression; righteousness, behold a cry—paronomasia in the Hebrew. Piety is described from the second table: where cruelty reigns, religion is extinguished. We who were wild olives grafted in (Rom 11) owe the same fruit.

“Vineyard”—Israel and Judah, then the church after them. Lord of hosts, house of Israel, Judah, justice, bloodshed, righteousness, outcry.
